title: Al-Nawawi's forty
hook: a Syrian scholar gathers the hadith on which the religion turns
tomorrow: the first hadith on his list is about something nobody can see. what?

segments.voice: A week of looking back and one step up. Keep asking. They were careful. Untitled teachers. Someone knows more. All roads face the qiblah. And yesterday, at the foot of the last range: now, the sources. Here's the first one.
screen: `KEEP ASKING · THEY WERE CAREFUL · UNTITLED TEACHERS` → `SOMEONE KNOWS MORE · ALL ROADS FACE THE QIBLAH` → `NOW, THE SOURCES.`

segments.voice: One carry-on bag for a long trip. Everything else stays home. Packing like that is mostly saying no: the third pair of shoes, the book you won't finish. What's left is what the whole trip rests on. Yesterday ended on a question: why would one scholar pick a short list for the whole faith? Because a short list is how you carry something that big. A scholar from Syria, al-Nawawi, sat down with the huge library of reports about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and packed one small bag.
screen: `ONE CARRY-ON.` → `PACKING IS SAYING NO.` → `ONE SMALL BAG FOR A HUGE LIBRARY.`

segments.voice: The word is arba'in, Arabic for forty. In his introduction, al-Nawawi says scholars before him had gathered forties of their own, each on one theme or another. He wanted something else: hadith that are each a foundation, reports scholars had called the axis the religion turns on, or half of it, or a third. So the list isn't one topic. It's a set of load-bearing walls in a house: pull one out, and a lot of rooms come down with it. Each day of this block opens one wall and looks at what it holds up. One thing to tell a friend tonight: count them, and the forty comes to forty-two. The name stayed; the bag got two more things. And he's honest about why he gathered them at all. A famous report promises a reward for whoever preserves forty hadith, and al-Nawawi admits the scholars agree its chains are weak. So he leans on a sound one instead, from the Prophet's farewell: let the one who is present pass it on to the one who is absent. That's the whole idea of a forty. Small enough to carry, solid enough to pass on. Forty-two foundations.
screen: `ARBA'IN: FORTY.` · `NOT A TOPIC: FOUNDATIONS.` · `COUNT THEM: FORTY-TWO.` · `PASS IT TO THE ONE WHO IS ABSENT.` · then, large: `FORTY-TWO FOUNDATIONS.`

segments.voice: Take a scrap of paper and write by hand the three things you'd pack if a younger cousin could carry only three from everything this path has given you. Short lines, no explaining, nothing clever: just what you'd want them to still have years from now. Then rest your hand on the list for the sit and read it once more, slowly.
screen: `A SCRAP OF PAPER.` · `THREE THINGS TO PACK.`

segments.voice: Arba'in. Forty, in Arabic, and the name of a whole kind of book: a short collection made to be learned and passed on. Al-Nawawi's is the one this block opens, one hadith at a time.
To pack for today: forty-two foundations, small enough to carry and meant to be passed on. A full week, done.

screen: `DAY 1428 COUNTS.` → `YEAR FIVE · 2 OF 365.` → `TOMORROW: THE FIRST HADITH ON HIS LIST IS ABOUT SOMETHING NOBODY CAN SEE.`

howItsDone: Al-Nawawi's Forty is studied in mosques, schools and homes; students often memorize it in Arabic and read it with a commentary, and copies are easy to find in bookstores, libraries and free editions online.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 (recipe v3): review shape. The review segment brings back the carries of days 1422–1427; games.recall holds all six for the review round. Today's word (arba'in) is taught lightly.

Al-Nawawi's introduction (paraphrased): earlier scholars compiled forties on various themes (he names many); he chose hadith each a great foundation, described by scholars as the axis of Islam, or half or a third of it; the 'whoever preserves forty hadith' report is weak by the agreement of the hadith masters, though he notes scholars permit acting on weak reports in virtuous deeds, and he relies on 'let the one present convey to the absent' and 'may Allah brighten one who hears my words…'. Confirm the paraphrase and that it is fair to say he 'leans on' the sound report.
'Let the one who is present pass it on to the one who is absent': Sahih al-Bukhari 67 (and 105, 1741) from the farewell sermon; confirm numbering.

'Forty-two' is the count of hadith in the standard text of al-Arba'in al-Nawawiyyah (the carry); Ibn Rajab later extended it to fifty, not mentioned. 'A scholar from Syria' follows the outline (al-Nawawi of Nawa, near Damascus); no dates given per the claims rule.
The outline practice 'find a copy of the forty' moved to howItsDone; the sit uses a handwritten 'pack three things' list instead.
